openingProblem.problem: In 1976 many Argentines accepted a military coup as the end of chaos. Seven years later the same military handed power to an elected president, who ordered its leaders to be prosecuted. Why did the dictatorship collapse, and on what foundations did the new democracy build?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what brought the dictatorship down?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: From Perón to the coup, 1946–1976
chunks.body:
Argentina had little experience of stable democracy. Between 1930 and 1983 it had numerous military coups, 25 presidents and 22 years of military rule. Its dominant political force was **Peronism**. Juan Perón built a mass following among trade unions from the 1940s, was overthrown by the military in 1955, and returned after eighteen years of exile to win the presidency again in 1973. He died a year later. His widow and successor, **Isabel Perón**, had little political experience. Economic and political chaos followed: political violence surged and Argentina suffered its first bout of hyperinflation.

The violence came from both sides. The *Nunca Más* report of 1984 describes a country "torn by terror from both the extreme right and the far left" in the 1970s. On **24 March 1976** the armed forces overthrew Isabel Perón. Congress was suspended, political parties were banned and civil rights were restricted. The junta called its regime the **Process of National Reorganization** (*el Proceso*).

The new government promised order and economic recovery. General **Jorge Videla** left the economy to José Alfredo Martínez de Hoz, who introduced free trade and deregulation. But the foreign debt increased fourfold during his tenure, and the gap between rich and poor grew much wider.

This mattered because many Argentines first accepted military rule as a response to chaos, which meant that the demand for democracy grew only when the regime itself was seen to have failed.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Argentina had a long tradition of military intervention.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Peronism had a large democratic following.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Chaos under Isabel Perón opened the way to the coup.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Violence came from both left and right.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The junta's economic policy failed to bring lasting recovery.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It ended shortages and the black market.

useItInAnEssay.prove: After Perón's death in 1974, political violence surged and Argentina suffered its first bout of hyperinflation; on 24 March 1976 the armed forces seized power.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the military could present itself as restoring order, so Congress was suspended and parties banned with little resistance.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Argentina had a long history of coups, with 22 years of military rule between 1930 and 1983, so 1976 continued a pattern rather than breaking one.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The coup was therefore the product both of immediate chaos and of a weak democratic tradition.

chunks.title: The Proceso: state terror, 1976–1981
chunks.body:
The junta claimed to be fighting a war against subversion. In practice, as CONADEP later found, it built a **planned system of repression**. The typical sequence was "abduction - disappearance - torture". People were seized by security forces who hid their identity and taken to one of some **340 secret detention centres**, run by senior officers. Many were murdered and their bodies destroyed so they could never be identified.

The victims were not only armed guerrillas. CONADEP found that thousands had no link with terrorism: trade unionists, students, journalists, intellectuals, priests and nuns, or simply relatives and friends of suspects. A US Embassy officer reported that the security forces were targeting people who, "in Videla's definition", were guilty of "bad thoughts". Women were among the disappeared, and 10 per cent of the women who disappeared were pregnant.

The regime also controlled public life. It closed the legislature, imposed severe censorship, and used the **1978 World Cup**, which Argentina hosted and won, as nationalist propaganda. Opposition came from victims' families. The **Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo** demanded to know where their children were. Between 8 and 10 December 1977, one of their founders, Azucena Villaflor de Vicenti, and eleven others, including two French nuns, were kidnapped by government forces and never seen again. Abroad, President Carter's administration secured a cutoff of US arms transfers in 1978.

CONADEP listed **8,960** disappeared people, while stressing that the true figure was higher; Argentine human rights groups estimate up to 30,000.

This mattered because the junta relied on secret terror rather than open law, which meant that, once it fell, the demand for democracy became inseparable from the demand for truth about the disappeared.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The junta claimed it was fighting a war.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Most victims had no link to terrorism.
Families of the disappeared led the opposition.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The regime silenced them by force.

useItInAnEssay.judge: Terror was therefore the main method of control, supported by propaganda and censorship.

chunks.title: Defeat and collapse, 1981–1983
chunks.body:
By the early 1980s the regime was in trouble. In 1981 General Viola was removed in a "palace coup" by General **Leopoldo Galtieri**. Facing military rivals and a failing economy, Galtieri planned a dramatic gamble: the invasion of the **Falkland Islands** (Islas Malvinas), long claimed by Argentina. The invasion in April 1982 gave the junta a huge boost in popularity. But a British naval task force retook the islands, and Argentina surrendered in June. The military, the US Congressional Research Service concludes, "fell into disrepute".

The economy was in deep crisis. Six years of intermittent wage freezes had left real wages around 40 per cent lower, and GDP per capita had fallen to its lowest level since 1968. When the new president, General **Reynaldo Bignone**, restored some freedoms, a wave of strikes followed, including two general strikes. On 16 December 1982 police repressed a mass demonstration in the Plaza de Mayo, killing one protester; Bignone's hope of postponing elections indefinitely was gone.

The junta prepared to protect itself. On 18 April 1983 it passed a **Self-Amnesty Law** and secretly ordered the destruction of records of its crimes. Elections were finally called for October 1983.

This mattered because military defeat destroyed the junta's claim to defend the nation, which meant that economic failure and public anger could no longer be held back by force.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Falklands defeat destroyed the junta's legitimacy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The invasion was popular at first.
Wage freezes had lasted six years.
The junta tried to protect itself with an amnesty.

useItInAnEssay.prove: Galtieri invaded the islands in April 1982 to boost the regime, but after the surrender in June, the CRS notes, the military 'fell into disrepute'.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the junta lost its claim to defend the nation, so it could no longer resist demands for elections.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the economy had already collapsed, with real wages around 40 per cent lower, and the invasion was itself a gamble by a failing regime.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The defeat was therefore the trigger, while economic failure was the underlying cause.

chunks.title: Alfonsín, CONADEP and Nunca Más, 1983–1984
chunks.body:
On **30 October 1983** Argentines voted in free elections, with a turnout of 85.6 per cent. **Raúl Alfonsín** of the Radical Civic Union (UCR), who had been among the first to condemn the military's self-amnesty, won 51.75 per cent of the vote, defeating the Peronist Ítalo Luder. He was sworn in on **10 December 1983**.

Alfonsín acted at once. On 13 December he ordered the prosecution of the nine officers of the first three juntas. Two days later he created the **National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons (CONADEP)**. Its members were chosen for their prestige and record of defending human rights, and the writer Ernesto Sabato was elected its president. CONADEP was not a court: its task was to establish the fate of the disappeared and pass evidence to the courts, not to judge guilt.

The commission worked against obstacles: records had been destroyed, and it was insulted and threatened by those it investigated. It prepared 7,380 files and gave the courts 1,086 dossiers on the main detention centres. On 20 September 1984 it presented its report, ***Nunca Más*** ("Never Again"). It concluded that the repression had been a deliberate plan, not a matter of "excesses", and recommended reparations for victims' families and compulsory human rights teaching. Sabato's prologue ended with a statement of democratic faith: "it is only democracy which can save a people from horror on this scale".

*Nunca Más* can be read in two ways. It is evidence about the dictatorship, based on thousands of testimonies. It is also evidence about how the new democracy chose to account for its past: by establishing the truth and leaving justice to the courts.

This mattered because the new democracy founded its legitimacy on truth about the disappeared, which meant that its later handling of justice for the military would test that commitment.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It could not determine individual responsibility.

useItInAnEssay.judge: The most significant result was therefore an official record that made denial impossible.

Families such as the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo had demanded answers, while the junta had passed a self-amnesty and destroyed records.
This meant that only an independent commission could rebuild the evidence, so CONADEP prepared 7,380 files and passed 1,086 dossiers to the courts.
However, CONADEP was not a court and could not determine responsibility, and it was accused of partiality.
The most significant result was therefore Nunca Más, which established the truth on which later justice depended.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the methods used by the military government to control Argentina between 1976 and 1983.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which method mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The junta controlled Argentina chiefly through secret terror, supported by the suspension of political life, censorship and nationalist propaganda.
modelPlan.counter: Families of the disappeared still protested, which shows the limits of control.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which mattered most? Secret terror, because it silenced opposition while denying responsibility.

segments.text: The military government's main method of control was secret terror.
CONADEP found a planned system of 'abduction - disappearance - torture' in some 340 secret detention centres, and listed 8,960 disappeared.
This meant that no one could feel safe, because the state denied all knowledge of its victims, so organised opposition was almost impossible.
However, the junta also relied on suspending Congress and parties, censorship and propaganda such as the 1978 World Cup, and the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo still protested.
Terror was therefore the core method, with propaganda and censorship making it harder to resist.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent did economic failure undermine the military government between 1976 and 1983?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Underlying cause, or one factor among several?

modelPlan.thesis: Economic failure seriously undermined the junta, as debt grew fourfold and real wages fell around 40 per cent, provoking strikes; but the decisive blow was the Falklands defeat.

arguments.claim: Protest in the Plaza de Mayo.

modelPlan.counter: The junta survived economic difficulties for years until the Falklands defeat.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How far? Economic failure weakened the junta; the defeat finished it.

segments.text: Economic failure was a major cause of the junta's decline.
Under Martínez de Hoz the foreign debt grew fourfold, and by 1983 wage freezes had left real wages around 40 per cent lower.
This meant that the regime lost its claim to bring prosperity, so when freedoms were restored, general strikes followed.
However, the junta survived its economic problems until the Falklands defeat of 1982 destroyed its legitimacy.
Economic failure therefore undermined the junta, but the defeat decided when it fell.
